answer_text:
Switching to the metric system in the US would be **extremely difficult** — though not impossible. Here's a comprehensive breakdown of the challenges involved:

---

## 🏛️ Historical Context

The US catches a lot of grief for never switching to the metric system, but the fact of the matter is, it tried several times. U.S. customary units have actually been defined in terms of metric units since the 19th century, and according to United States law, the metric system has been the "preferred system of weights and measures for United States trade and commerce" since 1975. The U.S. even has a national policy to adopt the metric system. Under Executive Order 12770, signed in 1991 by President George H.W. Bush, all U.S. agencies were required to adopt the metric system. However, conversion was made not mandatory, so U.S. customary units remain in common use in government and in many industries.

---

## 💸 The Core Problem: Cost and Infrastructure

The biggest reasons the U.S. hasn't adopted the metric system are simply time and money. When the Industrial Revolution began in the country, expensive manufacturing plants became a main source of American jobs and consumer products. Because the Imperial System was in place at this time, the machinery used in factories was developed to size in Imperial units, workers were trained to deal with Imperial units, and many products were made to feature Imperial units. Whenever the discussion of switching arose in Congress, the passage of a bill favoring the metric system was thwarted by big businesses and American citizens who didn't want to go through the time-consuming and expensive hassle of changing the country's entire infrastructure.

The US switching to metric this late in the game would be — by far — the largest, most complex transition of measurement systems in human history.

A 1926 Congressional debate illustrated just how sweeping the changes would be: It would be "chaos in industry" — grocers would have to get new scales, new measures; housewives would have to alter their recipes; gas meters, water meters, tape measures, and yardsticks would all have to be altered or replaced; measuring machines on counters would have to be reconstructed; new machinery devised for folding goods by meter instead of the yard.

---

## 🏫 Education Costs

The education system is perhaps the hardest hit. Both US Customary and Metric are taught, but students required to learn two measurement systems will likely be more confused, and the additional time spent teaching both systems has its own implied cost. On the flip side, one estimate found that metric calculations can generally be completed 45% faster, and a full conversion to a single measurement system could save roughly $17.6 billion.

---

## 🚀 The NASA Example

The cost of *not* converting can be dramatic. Over the course of a nine-month probe journey, a failure to use metric units in software led the craft to be around 170 kilometers lower than planned — that one mishap cost NASA $125 million. In 2015, NASA estimated a total conversion to the metric system would cost them $370 million — meaning the one-time conversion cost would be paid back relatively quickly.

---

## 🧠 Cultural Inertia and Political Resistance

There are real reasons for not switching that have nothing to do with American exceptionalism. For one, there's just cultural inertia — imagine what it would be like if all the numbers you used to measure your life suddenly changed.

Republican Charles Grassley killed proposed federal regulations that would have forced states to put up signs in kilometers, declaring: "Forcing the American people to convert to the metric system goes against our democratic principles." Many also believed that the United States should keep its particular system, setting it apart from other countries and symbolizing its status as a leader rather than a follower.

---

## ✅ The Silver Lining: Parts of the US Already Use Metric

Calling America a nonmetric nation is somewhat of a misnomer — the U.S. has given more than an inch. Coke bottles are sold in liters, so is wine, medicine is measured in milligrams, and food nutrition labels are already metric. Still, America is the only industrialized nation in the world that does not conduct business in metric weights and measures.

---

## 🔑 Bottom Line

A full US metrication would be **enormously difficult** — requiring massive overhauls to road signs, manufacturing equipment, legal standards, education curricula, and everyday consumer life. The biggest barriers are **cost, cultural resistance, and political will**, not technical feasibility. Countries like the UK and Australia managed it, but they did so much earlier in their industrial development. For the US today, it would require a long, phased, multi-decade commitment backed by strong (and unlikely) political consensus.
